reference.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students / Last's Anatomy
clinicalPearls: Composed of three unpaired cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis) and three paired cartilages (arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform)
Cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring in the entire human respiratory tract
Posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor of the vocal cords; bilateral paralysis causes life-threatening airway obstruction
Recurrent laryngeal nerve innervates all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid, which is supplied by the external superior laryngeal nerve
Left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch lateral to ligamentum arteriosum, vulnerable in mediastinal lymphadenopathy and thoracic aortic aneurysm
reference.pathophysiology: The larynx serves as an airway sphincter, phonatory oscillator and conduit for pulmonary ventilation. Intrinsic muscles alter tension, length and aperture of the vocal folds. Damage to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve causes monotone voice and loss of high-pitch projection. Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness with a paramedian cord; bilateral injury causes stridor.
additionalDifferentials: Vocal cord polyp or nodule (singer's nodule)
Squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx
Cricoarytenoid joint fixation in rheumatoid arthritis
additionalInvestigations: Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy to observe dynamic vocal cord mobility
Contrast-enhanced CT of neck and chest to trace recurrent laryngeal nerve course
Laryngeal electromyography (LEMG) for neurogenic vs mechanical immobility
